The pooling layer, which comes after the convolution layer, is meant to combine key information and lower the dimensionality of the feature map. Max pooling, which chooses the maximum value within each condensed area of the feature map, is a frequently used kind of pooling. This lessens the number of parameters that must be computed and increases the model's resistance to slight variations in the input features' locations.

CNNs typically have multiple sets of successive convolution and pooling layers, which allow the network to detect increasingly complex features at each layer. Early layers may detect simple edges and lines, while deeper layers may detect more complex objects, such as specific shapes and patterns.

The final input is supplied into the fully connected layer after passing through several convolution and pooling layers. Every neuron in this layer is connected to every other neuron in the layer before it, enabling the network to compile the features that were taken out of the earlier levels and come to a conclusion. An activation function that aids in the final classification, such as ReLU (Rectified Linear Unit) or Softmax, typically follows this completely connected layer.

This study designs and implements appropriate parameter values in each layer of the CNN used. The road damage detection research makes use of laser sensors to rebuild 3D road damage as well as stereo vision technologies. Several sensors are required for the stereo vision system, including two cameras, an LED, a laser, and LiDAR. The laser sensor has a small beamwidth; thus, it cannot detect road damage in the form of a large hole, necessitating the use of an array of LEDs, lasers, LiDARs, and other sensors [18], [49]. Reconstructing the pothole takes time, whether using an LED array, laser, or LiDAR. Furthermore, 3D road defect reconstruction and stereo vision require well-lit lighting and slow vehicle speeds [17], [18], [50].

Further research used image-processing techniques. Potholes are a form of road irregularity that can be recognized with traditional image processing techniques. To achieve high accuracy, this technique takes numerous steps, including manual image feature extraction and image processing parameter adjustments. As a result, the image frame rate varies depending on traffic circumstances [21]. Some research that investigated road conditions, pavement conditions, potholes, cracks, smart phone sensors, and accelerometers used machine learning techniques such as support vector machines, neural networks, multilayer perceptron, and decision trees [16]. Furthermore, research is being conducted to detect pavement damage using ML algorithms such as support vector machines, artificial neural networks, and random forests [51]. To improve accuracy, ML models require significant computer resources during data processing, which also includes manual feature analysis.

Several studies used deep convolutional neural network (CNN) techniques to automate the simultaneous feature extraction and categorization of objects [41], [52]. This is challenging to incorporate into real-time road defect detection systems. The deployment of CNN models for road damage detection on devices requires a balance between high accuracy and high efficiency [53]. The CNN models perform exceptionally well in terms of high accuracy, precision, recall, and low loss. This requires CNN models with large architecture and competitive computing costs that are inefficient. To do this while maintaining high accuracy, a simplified CNN model configuration setting is required to achieve good CNN model system performance. High efficiency, which is the CNN model system performance, enables it to detect road faults on edge devices with a short inference time. Because the CNN model on edge devices have limited storage capacity, inference time must be considered. Taking this into account, the CNN model offers good system performance and a short inference time for simpler model configurations, but high accuracy is difficult to achieve. To obtain optimal system performance, the CNN model parameters must be properly chosen. When selecting a detection model, there is no definitive answer as to which model has the best performance [31], [53].

Improving system performance in computer vision, object recognition, and classification using CNN models can be achieved through various methods. These include modifying or adding components to the CNN model structure and optimizing hyperparameter selection during CNN model training. The strategy of enhancing the CNN structure aims to improve feature extraction efficiency and model accuracy by modifying or incorporating new components into the CNN architecture. Several studies have focused on enhancing CNN models by modifying or adding components to the existing CNN structure [54], [55], [56], [57], [58], [59]. DenseNet was integrated into the YOLOv4 backbone to optimize feature transfer and reuse. This involved several modifications, such as adjusting the Path Aggregation Network (PANet) [54], introducing New Residual Blocks, applying Spatial Pyramid Pooling (SPP), modifying the PANet, and utilizing Hard-Swish activation functions [59]. Similarly, researchers have integrated DenseNet blocks into the YOLOv5 backbone to enhance the preservation and reuse of critical feature information. This was achieved by incorporating a Convolutional Block Attention Module (CBAM) [56]. Another study introduced a novel framework called Multiple Graph Learning Neural Networks (MGLNN) for semi-supervised learning on graph-based data [55]. Additionally, modifications were made to the YOLO model using the CSPDarknet53 backbone structure, which included Residual Blocks, DenseNet, Spatial Pyramid Pooling (SPP), and the Path Aggregation Network (PANet) [57].

This chapter discusses the results of the dataset that has been created as well as the results of the Convolutional Neural Network (CNN) testing that has been carried out. In this research, we produced a comprehensive dataset specifically designed for applications involving wheeled soccer goalkeeper robots. The dataset includes a variety of scenarios capturing different ball movements, speeds, shooting angles, and environmental conditions to ensure robustness and versatility.

The development, implementation, and compilation processes in this study were performed on a system with the specifications listed in Table 2. These specifications include various hardware components such as high-performance CPUs, GPUs, and adequate RAM, as well as software components including operating systems, deep learning frameworks, and data processing libraries. The choice of hardware and software was critical to achieve optimal performance, enabling efficient handling of complex algorithms and large volumes of data during the development, testing, and evaluation phases.

Using the right hardware ensured fast processing times and the ability to run intensive computations necessary for training deep learning models. Meanwhile, the selection of appropriate software provided the tools needed for data preprocessing, model training, and evaluation. For instance, the use of deep learning frameworks like TensorFlow facilitated the construction and training of the CNN model, while data processing libraries such as NumPy and Pandas were essential for managing and manipulating the dataset.

At epochs 0 to 20, training accuracy jumps significantly followed by a similar increase in validation accuracy. At epochs 21 to 40, there is a slight increase in training accuracy with a short period of decline before rising again, while validation accuracy rises significantly and then falls sharply before rising again. At epochs 41 to 60, both graphs show steady fluctuations. At epochs 61 to 80, the fluctuation pattern continued on both graphs. At the last epochs, 81 to 100, there is a significant drop in training accuracy followed immediately by a rapid rise, while validation accuracy shows a continuous up and down trend with no apparent stability. Testing was conducted to evaluate the performance of the trained model. Table 3 presents the performance report of the proposed model, a CNN-based machine learning model, in classifying test data into three categories: ''right,'' ''left,'' and ''center.'' With 180 test samples, the model achieved an overall accuracy of 70%, indicating that 70% of its predictions were correct. Table 3 shows the result of proposed method and other comparison models. From the performance evaluation results of the CNN prediction model for ball position, it was found that the model performed well for the prediction of the ''right'' and ''left'' classes, with F1-score of 0.84 and 0.76 respectively, indicating that the model was quite reliable in classifying both classes. However, the model performance for the ''center'' class showed a significant decrease, with an F1-score of only 0.39. This suggests either an imbalance in the data or a complexity in the ball movement pattern at the center that is difficult for the model to identify.

These findings show that while the CNN model is effective for most scenarios, there are areas that require improvement, especially in predicting the ''center'' class. One of the future development plans is to improve the data distribution by rebalancing the dataset so that the ''center'' class has more training examples. In addition, more complex models will be developed using other deep learning techniques, such as integration with Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM) to better capture temporal patterns in ball movement.

For the future, some other approaches that can be developed include the use of data augmentation to generate more variations of the ball position in the ''center'' class, as well as further tuning the CNN architecture to reduce the overfitting phenomenon detected in some epochs during training. The use of attention mechanisms can also be implemented to help the model focus on key features of the ball movement, so as to improve prediction accuracy, especially in the ''center'' class which tends to be less accurate.
